proposals.old: The success-tuned agents show the same effect more starkly. At their in-class tuned weights both drive reward to a near-zero $+0.01$ while reaching $99.5\%$ success, giving up almost the entire return to buy the last few points of accuracy. This is the one environment where the posterior-vote baseline exactly ties the best agent, and on Bandit it posts the highest mean reward of any agent. Posterior-vote matches reward-only Planning bit-for-bit ($+0.48$, $89.8\%$, $3.15$ observations), and both beat EFE on reward. The Epistemic-only ablation of Table~\ref{tab:agents}, which sets $\mathcal{G}(\text{commit}) = 0$, also observes $3.15$ times and succeeds at $89.8\%$ here, matching reward-only Planning exactly on both figures (\texttt{results\_\allowbreak summary.csv}), because Testbed's observation is cheap enough that information gain alone clears its cost. On Tiger, Diagnosis, Bandit, and Tileworld it instead commits immediately at the chance rate (Appendix~\ref{app:full_tables}). The testbed result is informative about the conditions under which $w{=}1$ is near-optimal. With symmetric $\pm 1$ rewards a second observation at the post-first-observation belief has zero instrumental value, since the disconfirming outcome returns the belief exactly to the tie point, so its $0.1$ cost buys no reward at all. Proposition~\ref{prop:nearopt}'s over-observation ceiling is correspondingly tight here, $w^*_{\mathrm{over}} \approx 1.01$ reward units per nat (Table~\ref{tab:alpha_eta}), which sits below the implemented bit-denominated $w{=}1$ at $1.44$ reward units per nat. The reward-optimal weight therefore falls below the canonical one. In this regime, EFE assigns too much weight to information gain. Many real-world decision problems, including medical diagnosis, fault detection, and security screening, have asymmetric penalties ($|R^-|/|R^+| \gg 1$), the regime in which the two-state interval analysis is most favorable to $w{=}1$. Within that regime, $w{=}1$ lies on the reward-maximizing plateau on Tiger and Diagnosis but is Pareto-dominated by $w{=}20$ on Tileworld (Section~\ref{sec:pareto}).

The Epistemic-only ablation of Table~\ref{tab:agents}, which sets $\mathcal{G}(\text{commit}) = 0$, also matches reward-only Planning on observations and success here (\texttt{results\_\allowbreak summary.csv}), because Testbed's observation is cheap enough that information gain alone clears its cost. On Tiger, Diagnosis, Bandit, and Tileworld it instead commits immediately at the chance rate (Appendix~\ref{app:full_tables}). With symmetric $\pm 1$ rewards a second observation at the post-first-observation belief has zero instrumental value, since the disconfirming outcome returns the belief exactly to the tie point, so its $0.1$ cost buys no reward. Proposition~\ref{prop:nearopt}'s over-observation ceiling is correspondingly tight, $w^*_{\mathrm{over}} \approx 1.01$ reward units per nat (Table~\ref{tab:alpha_eta}), below the implemented bit-denominated $w{=}1$ at $1.44$ reward units per nat, so in this regime EFE assigns too much weight to information gain. The high-asymmetry regime in which the interval analysis favors $w{=}1$ is discussed in Appendix~\ref{app:interpretation}. proposals.old: At $K{=}1$ all agents face the same single test, and EFE and Planning are bit-identical. At $K{=}2$ the two remain within seed-level sampling error of each other ($43.2\%$ against $43.8\%$ success), with the multi-test evidence at that scale carried by the main Diagnosis battery (Section~\ref{sec:results}). The separation opens at $K{=}3$ ($96.0\%$ against $82.8\%$, $+13.2$pp), because selecting among competing tests is what the information-gain term contributes. The pattern is a threshold rather than a steady growth. Figure~\ref{fig:extended_efe} shows the mechanism at work over a single extended episode. Tests become differentially informative as belief concentrates, since some partitions of the state space stop mattering once the condition is narrowed down while others remain decisive. The EFE agent changes its test selection as belief evolves. It optimizes a recursive pragmatic--epistemic score, so its chosen test need not maximize the one-step information gain plotted in panel (b). proposals.old: We check our EFE computation against the \texttt{pymdp} library \citep{heins2022} by wrapping pymdp's standard Agent class. This comparison checks consistency between implementations. It does not certify numerical equivalence, so the evidence below is stated in terms of the behaviors actually compared. The quantitative form of the check is a deployed comparison on the two-state testbed. Run as an ordinary observe-then-commit agent over the canonical protocol, \texttt{pymdp}-AIF returns $3.15$ observations, $89.8\%$ success, and $+0.480$ reward, bit-identical to reward-only Planning on all three metrics (\texttt{results\_\allowbreak summary.csv}). The meaningful comparator here is our own myopic Info Gain agent at $w{=}1$, which \texttt{results\_\allowbreak summary.csv} records at the same $3.15$ observations, $89.8\%$ success, and $+0.480$ reward. Both agents evaluate single-step policies, and by Proposition~\ref{prop:equivalence} the myopic $w{=}1$ agent is the myopic EFE agent. This is therefore a like-for-like agreement. Our $H{=}4$ recursive EFE agent legitimately differs on this environment ($5.50$ observations), through planning depth rather than through any disagreement about the epistemic term. The check is therefore evidence that the two myopic implementations agree, not that recursive EFE matches pymdp. It remains weak evidence, since on this environment the myopic $w{=}1$ agent is itself bit-identical to reward-only Planning, so the comparison cannot separate a correctly implemented epistemic term from its absence.
proposals.new: We check our EFE computation against the \texttt{pymdp} library \citep{heins2022} by wrapping pymdp's standard Agent class. The check tests consistency between implementations, not numerical equivalence. Run as an observe-then-commit agent on the two-state testbed under the canonical protocol, \texttt{pymdp}-AIF returns $3.15$ observations, $89.8\%$ success, and $+0.480$ reward. Our myopic Info Gain agent at $w{=}1$, which by Proposition~\ref{prop:equivalence} is the myopic EFE agent, returns the same three values (\texttt{results\_\allowbreak summary.csv}), so the two single-step implementations agree. Our $H{=}4$ recursive EFE agent differs on this environment ($5.50$ observations) through planning depth, so the check says nothing about recursive EFE. It is also weak evidence, because on this environment the myopic $w{=}1$ agent and \texttt{pymdp}-AIF are both bit-identical to reward-only Planning, so the comparison cannot separate a correctly implemented epistemic term from its absence.
proposals.rationale: Same numbers and the same three limitations (consistency not equivalence, myopic only, cannot distinguish the epistemic term from its absence) in about half the words. The triple statement of 3.15/89.8/+0.480 becomes one.

proposals.old: \paragraph{Agreement across planning horizons.} Figure~\ref{fig:nearopt_horizon} stratifies only by reward asymmetry $\alpha$. Table~\ref{tab:horizon-map} breaks the same 100 environments down by all three sampled regime axes and adds a direct per-environment comparison of the $H{=}1$ classification against $H{\geq}2$. Eight of the nine regime strata show the same qualitative pattern, with near-optimality rarer at $H{=}1$ than at $H{=}3$. The effect is sharpest for high-informativeness observations ($p \geq 0.85$, rising $17\% \to 90\%$). The exception is the low-informativeness stratum ($p < 0.65$, $25$ environments), which is flat and mildly non-monotone at $80\% \to 84\% \to 80\%$, since weak observations leave little for a deeper horizon to exploit. Low reward asymmetry rises but less sharply ($\alpha < 3$, from $71\%$ at $H{=}1$ to $86\%$ by $H{=}2$, holding there through $H{=}3$, on 7 environments). The per-environment comparison uses the producing script's definition of agreement. An environment agrees when $w{=}1$ is near-optimal at $H{=}1$ and at some deeper horizon, or at neither. By that definition the two horizons agree on 44 of the 100 environments. In 30 the $H{=}1$ check passes and near-optimality recurs at some deeper horizon. In 26 of those 30 it holds at every deeper horizon tested. In 14 the check fails and never recovers. The remaining 56 environments fail the $H{=}1$ check yet turn out near-optimal at some deeper horizon (myopic underclaiming, the safe direction, a missed opportunity rather than a risk). On this random sample, zero environments show the opposite pattern (myopic overclaiming, where $H{=}1$ predicts near-optimality but no deeper horizon delivers it). Four of the 30 passers fail at exactly one of the two deeper horizons (environments 2, 42, 63, and 95 in the committed CSV). A practitioner validating $w{=}1$ with a cheap $H{=}1$ check would therefore have been misled at one specific deeper horizon in 4 of 30 cases, and in no case toward a weight that fails at every deeper horizon. This is a property of the observed sample, not a proven guarantee. We report it as an empirical boundary map over one random family of two-state environments, not an adaptive-submodularity result. We make no claim that the $H{=}1$ check is monotone or that overclaiming is impossible in general, only that it did not occur here (the per-environment data is in \texttt{results/\allowbreak results\_\allowbreak nearopt\_\allowbreak horizon.csv}, from which \texttt{experiments/\allowbreak build\_\allowbreak horizon\_\allowbreak map.py} derives the aggregate agreement counts in \texttt{results/\allowbreak results\_\allowbreak horizon\_\allowbreak map\_\allowbreak agreement.csv}).
proposals.new: \paragraph{Agreement across planning horizons.} Table~\ref{tab:horizon-map} breaks the same 100 environments down by all three sampled regime axes and compares the $H{=}1$ classification with $H{\geq}2$ per environment. Eight of the nine regime strata show near-optimality rarer at $H{=}1$ than at $H{=}3$, most sharply for high-informativeness observations ($p \geq 0.85$, $17\% \to 90\%$). The exception is the low-informativeness stratum ($p < 0.65$, $25$ environments), flat and mildly non-monotone at $80\% \to 84\% \to 80\%$, since weak observations leave little for a deeper horizon to exploit. Low reward asymmetry ($\alpha < 3$, 7 environments) rises less sharply, from $71\%$ at $H{=}1$ to $86\%$ at both $H{=}2$ and $H{=}3$. Following the producing script, an environment agrees when $w{=}1$ is near-optimal at $H{=}1$ and at some deeper horizon, or at neither, which holds for 44 of the 100. In 30 the $H{=}1$ check passes and near-optimality recurs deeper, at every deeper horizon in 26 of them and at exactly one of the two in the other four (environments 2, 42, 63, and 95 in the committed CSV). In 14 the check fails and never recovers. The remaining 56 fail at $H{=}1$ yet are near-optimal at some deeper horizon, a missed opportunity rather than a risk. proposals.old: We test EFE and Planning agents' sensitivity to discounting by sweeping $\gamma \in \{0.9, 0.95, 0.99, 1.0\}$ across three environments, at the canonical 5-seed protocol. Including Planning at each $\gamma$ enables comparison of the relative gap between agents under discounting.
proposals.new: We sweep $\gamma \in \{0.9, 0.95, 0.99, 1.0\}$ for EFE and same-horizon Planning on three environments under the canonical 5-seed protocol, so that the gap between the two agents can be read at each discount.
proposals.rationale: Tighter wording with the same content.

proposals.old: On Diagnosis and Bandit, heavy discounting ($\gamma{=}0.9$--$0.95$) renders both agents effectively myopic, erasing EFE's advantage entirely. At $\gamma{=}0.9$--$0.95$, EFE's epistemic term cannot propagate value through future observations because discounting truncates the effective horizon below the number of observations needed for disambiguation. Both agents observe the same number of times on Bandit (${\sim}2$) and Diagnosis (${\sim}6$) at these discount levels, and the residual success gaps are not statistically significant (Diagnosis diff $\approx 0.04$pp, $p{=}0.96$, Bandit diff $\approx -0.16$pp, $p{=}0.95$, Table~\ref{tab:discount}). The transition between $\gamma{=}0.95$ and $\gamma{=}0.99$ is sharp and, with 5-seed replication, clearly significant. At $\gamma{=}0.99$, EFE's success gap over Planning jumps to $+7.9$ pp on Diagnosis and $+22.4$ pp on Bandit (both $p<10^{-4}$), matching the undiscounted pattern ($+8.6$ pp Diagnosis, $+17.0$ pp Bandit at $\gamma{=}1.0$, both $p<10^{-4}$). This confirms that EFE's advantage depends on the discount factor preserving a sufficient effective horizon for recursive epistemic evaluation. In practical terms, on the multi-observation environments Diagnosis and Bandit, EFE differentiates from reward-only planning on success at the two largest discount factors tested, $\gamma \in \{0.99, 1.0\}$, and not at $\gamma \in \{0.90, 0.95\}$, so the transition lies between $0.95$ and $0.99$ on this grid, and the 5-seed replication makes the significance of that transition a confirmed finding rather than a single-seed point estimate.
proposals.new: On Diagnosis and Bandit, heavy discounting ($\gamma{=}0.9$--$0.95$) renders both agents effectively myopic and erases EFE's advantage, because discounting truncates the effective horizon below the number of observations needed for disambiguation. Both agents observe the same number of times on Bandit (${\sim}2$) and Diagnosis (${\sim}6$) at these discount levels, and the residual success gaps are not statistically significant (Diagnosis diff $\approx 0.04$pp, $p{=}0.96$, Bandit diff $\approx -0.16$pp, $p{=}0.95$, Table~\ref{tab:discount}). The transition between $\gamma{=}0.95$ and $\gamma{=}0.99$ is sharp, and the gaps at $\gamma \geq 0.99$ are significant after Holm correction. At $\gamma{=}0.99$, EFE's success gap over Planning jumps to $+7.9$ pp on Diagnosis and $+22.4$ pp on Bandit (both $p<10^{-4}$), matching the undiscounted pattern ($+8.6$ pp Diagnosis, $+17.0$ pp Bandit at $\gamma{=}1.0$, both $p<10^{-4}$). On this grid, EFE's advantage therefore requires a discount that preserves a sufficient effective horizon for recursive epistemic evaluation.
proposals.rationale: Removes history narration ('with 5-seed replication', 'a confirmed finding rather than a single-seed point estimate', which alludes to a superseded single-seed sweep), the overclaiming 'This confirms', and a closing 'In practical terms' sentence that restates the paragraph and app:interpretation. The significance is now tied to the Holm correction the table actually marks.

proposals.old: On Tiger, success falls at most $2.7$pp below the calibrated $99.6\%$ for both EFE and Planning across the tested range of $-0.15$ to $+0.10$. The degradation pattern is asymmetric. For EFE and Planning, negative mismatch (underestimating accuracy, including exact calibration) leaves observation count and success unchanged (4.23 observations, 99.6\% success at every level from $-0.15$ to $0.00$), whereas positive mismatch (overestimating accuracy) sharply reduces observation count (to 2.65) and lowers success to 96.9\%. EFE and Planning give bit-identical rows at every mismatch level tested on Tiger (Table~\ref{tab:misspec-tiger}), not merely statistically indistinguishable ones. With a single observation action, the belief-update dynamics driven by the agent's believed accuracy determine when committing becomes attractive, and information gain has no separate observation action to redirect toward. There is therefore no EFE-specific buffering effect to report here. This finding is specific to the tested environment and cannot be attributed to the epistemic term. The same asymmetric degradation appears in reward-only Planning, which has no information-gain term at all.
proposals.new: On Tiger, success falls at most $2.7$pp below the calibrated $99.6\%$ across the tested range of $-0.15$ to $+0.10$, and the pattern is asymmetric. Underestimating accuracy or calibrating exactly leaves behavior unchanged (4.23 observations, 99.6\% success at every level from $-0.15$ to $0.00$), whereas overestimating it cuts observations to 2.65 and success to 96.9\%. EFE and Planning give bit-identical rows at every tested level (Table~\ref{tab:misspec-tiger}), not merely statistically indistinguishable ones. With a single observation action, the believed accuracy alone determines when committing becomes attractive, and information gain has no separate observation action to redirect toward. The study therefore shows no EFE-specific buffering on Tiger, since reward-only Planning, with no information-gain term, degrades identically.
proposals.rationale: Four sentences saying there is no EFE-specific effect become one. It also removes the confusing phrase 'negative mismatch (..., including exact calibration)'.

proposals.old: This is not a ``well-calibrated agent tests most, both directions of error reduce testing'' pattern. Perfect calibration ($\pm 0.00$) ties with two levels of underestimation rather than uniquely maximizing testing, and only the most extreme underestimate tested ($-0.15$) drops to the low-testing level, matching every overestimate we tested. Overestimating accuracy (the agent believes tests are more informative than they truly are) makes each test look more decisive than it is, so the agent commits prematurely on insufficient evidence and lands in the low-testing, lower-success regime at every overestimate level tested. Underestimating accuracy makes each test look less informative than it is, but only past a threshold. Mild underestimation ($-0.05$, $-0.10$) does not visibly change behavior from perfect calibration, while severe underestimation ($-0.15$) triggers the same reduced-testing response as overestimation, producing a similar-looking success rate (88.7\%) that is, as before, driven by fewer rather than more observations.
